turns.t: Come in, have a seat. Before we start, how would you like me to address you?
Oh, Priya is fine. Everyone calls me that. Mrs Nair feels like my mother-in-law.
Priya it is. I see you're here for your multiple sclerosis review. How have things been since we last met?
Mostly stable, I think. But I'm worried, doctor, because I'm just so tired all the time now.
Tell me more about the tiredness. Is it sleepiness, or more a heavy, drained feeling?
Drained. I wake up after eight hours and still feel like I've run a marathon.
And when did you first notice the fatigue? Roughly.
Um, that's the thing, I can't say. Maybe around Christmas, or was it before the summer? I honestly don't know.
That's fine, it often creeps in slowly. Does it get worse at certain times of day?
Afternoons are the worst. Is this a relapse? Is the MS getting worse? I keep lying awake thinking about it.
Good question, and I'll come back to it. First, any new numbness, tingling or weakness in your arms or legs?
No, nothing new. My legs feel the same as always.
Any change in your eyesight, like blurring or pain when you move your eyes?
No, my eyes have been fine. I'd have rushed in if they weren't.
Good. Now, let me check your medicines. What are you taking at the moment?
The levothyroxine, 75 micrograms, every morning on an empty stomach. And a vitamin D, 1000 units once a day.
Right. Anything else, even from the chemist? Herbal things, painkillers?
No, just those two. Oh, and I do worry that I forget the vitamin D some days.
Don't fret about that, a missed day here and there matters very little.
Okay. Should I be taking something stronger for the tiredness?
Not yet. There are lots of reasons for tiredness in MS, so I want to look at the whole picture first.
What sort of reasons?
Thyroid levels, vitamin levels, anaemia, poor sleep, low mood. Your thyroid has been underactive for a while, hasn't it?
Yes, my underactive thyroid, it's been about eight years now. And the MS was diagnosed six years ago.
Thank you. Any operations in the past that I should know about?
Only my appendix, about fifteen years ago. Nothing since.
Okay. And just so I have it right for your record, do you have any allergies to medicines?
No, none that I know of. I've never had a reaction to anything.
Lovely. Let's get your observations done now. Sam will help with the scales first.
Hello, Priya. Could you step onto the scales for me, shoes off, please?
Of course. Oh dear, I hope it hasn't gone up.
It's fine, don't worry. Back to the chair when you're ready, and the doctor will take the rest.
Your blood pressure is 118 over 76, and your pulse is 68 and regular.
Is that good? It sounded a bit fast when I counted at home.
That's a perfectly comfortable pulse. Temperature is 36.7 degrees, and oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
And the weight I took was 64 kilograms. Same as last time, I believe.
Yes, that matches. So no big changes, which is reassuring.
So what happens now? I really don't want to just go home and carry on feeling like this.
I'd like to arrange a blood test today, covering your thyroid function, vitamin D, iron and blood count.
And if those are all normal? I'd be so frustrated.
Then we look at sleep, mood and pacing your day. Fatigue is real, and we'd treat it as real.
That helps to hear. I sometimes feel everyone thinks I'm just lazy.
Nobody here does. I'll ring you with the results, and we can talk through next steps together.
Priya, pop by my desk afterwards and I'll hand you the blood form and show you the way to the phlebotomy room.
Will do. Thank you, doctor, I feel a little less panicky than when I walked in.
Good. Be kind to yourself, Priya.
I'll try. Bye for now.
Goodbye.
